title: Humanoid Robots Are Entering the Workforce

slides.heading: Humanoid Robots Are Entering the Workforce
slides.body: How machines shaped like us are transforming factories, warehouses, and beyond

slides.heading: From Sci-Fi to Factory Floor
slides.body: Once confined to movies and research labs, humanoid robots are now active in real workplaces. Companies like Tesla, Boston Dynamics, and Agility Robotics have deployed bipedal robots that walk, carry, and sort — alongside human colleagues.

slides.heading: Why Human-Shaped Robots?
slides.body: Our world is built for human bodies — stairs, shelves, tools, and vehicles all assume an upright form. Humanoid robots can operate in existing facilities without costly redesigns, giving them a massive practical advantage over other automation approaches.

slides.heading: Who's Leading the Race?
slides.body: Tesla's Optimus, Figure AI's Figure 02, and Agility's Digit are competing for early industrial contracts. Meanwhile, Chinese firms like Unitree are flooding the market with lower-cost alternatives, intensifying global competition.

slides.heading: What Jobs Are They Doing?
slides.body: Current deployments focus on repetitive, physically demanding tasks: picking and packing boxes, loading trucks, assembling parts, and restocking shelves. These are roles with high turnover and injury rates — making them prime targets for automation.

slides.heading: The Role of AI in Giving Robots a Brain
slides.body: Modern humanoids run on large neural networks trained with reinforcement learning and real-world demonstrations. They can generalize to new objects and layouts without being explicitly programmed — a leap that was impossible just five years ago.

slides.heading: Economics: Are They Cost-Effective?
slides.body: Today's humanoid robots cost $30,000–$150,000 each, with additional maintenance and programming expenses. Analysts project costs dropping 60–80% by 2030, potentially making them cheaper than minimum-wage labor in high-cost markets.

slides.heading: Human Impact: Jobs Lost or Transformed?
slides.body: Economists disagree on net job effects. Warehousing and logistics are most exposed in the short term. History suggests automation creates new roles — but the transition is painful for affected workers without retraining support.

slides.heading: Safety and Regulation Challenges
slides.body: Working alongside humans, humanoid robots raise new safety standards. Regulators in the EU and US are drafting robot-in-workplace rules covering collision avoidance, liability, and mandatory human oversight zones.

slides.heading: The Robot Colleague Era Has Begun
slides.body: Humanoid robots are no longer a future promise — they're clocking in today. Understanding how they work, where they'll be deployed, and how to adapt will be the defining skill of the next decade.
